points.text: The instruction fine-tuning project has already completed data set preparation and fine-tuning, and the next stage is evaluating the large language model.
The instruction data set consists of 1,100 instruction, input, and output pairs.
The data was split into 85% for training, 10% for testing, and 5% for validation.
The model was initialized with publicly available GPT-2 weights to provide a good foundational base before fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning means training the large language model again so that it learns from the instruction input-output data set and becomes better at responding to instructions.
In the demonstrated run, the model was trained for only one epoch because of memory and compute limitations on the lecturer's CPU.
Running the fine-tuning for more epochs, such as two instead of one, can improve the quality of the model's responses.
For the passive-voice example, the fine-tuned model answered "the meal is prepared by the chef every day," which is better than random output but not the correct answer.
Evaluating a large language model is challenging because performance is not a simple yes-or-no classification and requires comparing generated sentences with target sentences.
The evaluation process in this lecture is organized into three stages: extracting responses from the model, qualitative evaluation, and scoring the responses.
To evaluate the model on the test set, first generate the model's response for every test input and collect those responses for manual analysis and later comparison with the ground-truth outputs.

The code loops over the test data, selects the first three entries, generates outputs with the fine-tuned model, converts token IDs to text, removes the instruction and input portion from the generated text, and prints the instruction, the correct response, and the model response.
For the test prompt about rewriting a sentence using a simile, the model response "the car is as fast as a bullet" is very close to the correct response "the car is as fast as lightning."
For the question asking which cloud type is associated with thunderstorms, the model response is not good because it does not provide the requested cloud type.
For the question asking for the author of Pride and Prejudice, the model answer "George Bernard Shaw" is clearly wrong because the correct answer is Jane Austen.
From the three sample outputs, the first answer is close to correct, the second does not answer correctly, and the third is fully wrong.
Qualitative inspection can show whether responses seem correct or incorrect, but it does not by itself provide a numerical evaluation score.
Evaluation for instruction-tuned language models is harder than spam-versus-not-spam classification, where accuracy is easy to compute from whether the predicted label matches the correct label.

Large language model evaluation is an important and rapidly developing field because without evaluation metrics it is hard to know what is good, what is bad, and whether research is progressing successfully.
One common way to evaluate instruction fine-tuned language models is to benchmark them on a general knowledge test called MMLU, which stands for Massive Multitask Language Understanding.
An MMLU score is a score that tests the general knowledge of a model across a wide range of questions in different fields.

The lecturer shows the MMLU paper and points to a list of 57 tasks or subject areas, such as abstract algebra, anatomy, astronomy, business ethics, biology, chemistry, computer science, law, management, marketing, and public relations.

According to the summarized description shown on screen, MMLU is a benchmark for measuring language model knowledge and evaluating a text model's ability to learn and apply knowledge from various domains.
MMLU consists of 57 tasks that cover STEM, humanities, social sciences, and other areas, with difficulty ranging from elementary to professional levels.

MMLU can be used to evaluate a custom instruction fine-tuned LLM by testing its performance on those 57 tasks, and many instruction fine-tuning research papers report the MMLU score as a measure of general knowledge performance.
One approach to evaluating LLMs is human preference comparison, in which humans examine answers from multiple LLMs and compare their performance.
Human preference comparison puts a human in the loop, and the human uses their own intuition and understanding to benchmark or compare LLMs.
A third common approach to evaluating LLMs is to use another large language model to compare the expected output with the model response and assign a score.
Using an LLM as the evaluator is fairly straightforward because it is fully automated.
Using an LLM to score responses is like taking the easy way out because the evaluation criteria used by the LLM are not known, so the method relies on trusting the evaluator LLM.
In this lecture, the chosen evaluation method is to give an LLM the true output and the model response, ask it to compare them, and assign a score.

Automatically evaluating responses with another LLM can efficiently assess response quality without extensive human involvement, saving time and resources while still producing meaningful performance indicators.
The lecturer would like someone to run the MMLU test code on the instruction fine-tuned LLM if possible.
The next step is to collect model responses for all instructions in the test dataset and store those responses in a separate file for evaluation.
The evaluation preparation creates a new file called instruction data with response.json for record keeping.
The instruction data with response file contains the instruction, the input, the true output, and the model response.

The original instruction data.json file is shown as containing only the instruction, input, and true output, while the new instruction data with response file is shown as also including the model response.
Having a file with both the true output and the model response makes later evaluation easier because each pair can be compared and scored directly.
The code iterates over all instruction inputs in the test data, generates responses for them, and writes the results to the instruction data with response file.
When this code runs, the generate function is called on all instruction-input pairs in the test data, and the generated response is appended to the instruction data with response file.
The resulting instruction data with response file is shown as the original instruction-input-output dictionary with an added model response field for every example.
Creating the instruction data with response file can take time; in the lecturer's case it took around 10 to 15 minutes.
After this process, the test data dictionary contains the instruction, input, output, and model response.
After preparing the evaluation file, the fine-tuned model should be saved so the session can be resumed later without fine-tuning again.
The model is saved using torch.save with model.state_dict, which stores the trained parameters in a file.
To load the model in a future session, load_state_dict is used to load the saved parameter file.
At this stage, the responses have been collected in instruction data with response.json, the three evaluation frameworks have been discussed, and the LLM-based comparison framework has been selected.
Earlier work included extracting responses and doing qualitative evaluation by looking at outputs and responses, but numerical scoring has not yet been implemented.
After extracting responses from the fine-tuned LLM, another large language model will be used to automatically evaluate those responses.
The evaluation will use a larger pre-trained LLM to compare the model response with the true response and assign a score.
Ollama is software or an application used to run large language models on a laptop efficiently.
With Ollama, various large language models such as Llama 3, Phi-3, Mistral, and Gemma 2 can be run on a PC.
Ollama is used for inference only, not for pre-training.
The evaluation step will use an instruction-fine-tuned Llama 3 8 billion parameter model accessed through Ollama.
The reason for using the instruction-fine-tuned Llama 3 8B model is that it has already been fine-tuned on many instructions and is trained to follow instructions well.
The Llama 3 8B instruction-fine-tuned model will be instructed to compare the actual output with the model response and assign a score.
Because the Llama model is already trained to follow instructions, it is expected to do a great job on the new instruction of producing an evaluation score.
Ollama is a commonly used LLM inference application.
Ollama is only a tool for generating text with LLM inference and does not support training or fine-tuning.
To install Ollama, go to ollama.com, click download, download the version for your operating system, and follow the installation steps.
The Ollama download file shown for macOS is 177 MB, and the installation process is simple and does not take much time.
After installing Ollama, open a terminal and run the command ollama run llama3.
On Windows, first run ollama serve and then run ollama run llama3.
When running Llama 3 through Ollama, the downloaded files are 4.7 GB because the model has 8 billion parameters, so it requires substantial space and memory.
Downloading the Llama 3 model through Ollama took around 15 to 20 minutes for the lecturer.
During the model download, instructions are printed in the terminal, and after a successful load, right-side arrows appear to show that Llama 3 is ready for interaction.
Once Llama 3 is loaded in Ollama, it can be interacted with by asking it questions.
Ollama lets you run local large language models such as Llama 3, Phi-3, Mistral, and Gemma 2 on your laptop.
You must keep Ollama running while executing the later code, because if you shut down the terminal then Ollama stops and the code will not execute.
A simple way to test whether Ollama is running is to ask it a question and check whether it returns a response.

Before using Ollama to evaluate test set responses, you should run a verification code block and confirm that it prints "Ollama running = true"; if it prints false, Ollama is not running successfully.
The purpose of the evaluation is to use Ollama with Llama 3 to compare the correct output with the model response and assign a score.
A `query_model` function can be used from Python to interact with a Llama model through the API instead of repeatedly running `ollama run llama3` in the terminal.
The `query_model` function takes a prompt and a model, sends an API request to that model based on the prompt, and returns the generated response.
In this evaluation setup, the prompt sent through `query_model` asks the evaluator model to compare the output and the model response and assign a score.
Before running later code cells, you should again confirm that Ollama is still active by checking that the earlier test prints "Ollama running = True".
A demo of `query_model` passes a prompt such as "what do llamas eat" together with a model like Llama 3, and then prints the model's response.
The lecturer uses the Llama 3 8B instruction-tuned model because it is already fine-tuned on instruction data.
Querying local models through Ollama can require substantial compute and memory, can be slow on CPU, and may require freeing 15 to 20 GB of memory for the code to run.
On limited hardware, multiple simultaneous queries can cause the laptop to hang, so the lecturer could handle at most about two queries in one session.
To evaluate fine-tuned model responses, you should prompt Llama 3 to rate the fine-tuned model's response against the given test response on a scale from 0 to 100.

The evaluation prompt should include the instruction and input, the correct output, and the model response, and ask the evaluator model to score the response on a scale of 0 to 100 where 100 is the best score.
This approach uses one large language model, Llama 3 8B, to evaluate another fine-tuned large language model.
If no model is specified when calling `query_model`, it uses Llama 3 by default.
The evaluation code shown tests three data points, printing each model response and the score assigned by the Llama model.
On the lecturer's laptop, running the evaluation for three test samples initially caused a crash and then took about 35 minutes, making evaluation of the full test set impractical.

In the first example, the evaluator model gave a score of 85 out of 100 because the response used a simile correctly and captured the intended meaning, even though it was less vivid than the reference answer.
In the second example, the evaluator model gave a score of 20 out of 100 because the response did not directly answer the question, was largely irrelevant, and contained inaccuracies.
In the third example, the evaluator model gave a score of 0 out of 100 because the answer was factually incorrect and irrelevant.
The lecturer judges the evaluator model to be strong at qualitative evaluation and finds its quantitative scores generally sensible enough to trust.
Llama 3 can provide reasonable evaluations and can assign partial credit as well as zero when an answer is incorrect.
If you want only a numeric metric instead of a qualitative explanation, you can change the prompt to instruct the evaluator model to respond with an integer number only.
Using another LLM to score an LLM gives a quantitative metric, but it is less robust and more subjective than classification accuracy.

LLM evaluation is an open research area because there is substantial subjectivity in choosing metrics and in judging responses, unlike tasks with a single accuracy value based on right and wrong answers.
A function is provided that can iterate over the entire test set, compute a score of this kind for every instruction, and then calculate an average score.
The lecturer does not run the full-test-set scoring function because of hardware limitations, but notes that faster hardware such as an M3 MacBook Air or a GPU can run it much more quickly.
When the full evaluation code is run, the fine-tuned model achieves an average score above 50, which can serve as a benchmark for comparing other models or training configurations.
Ollama is not entirely deterministic, so the scores you obtain may differ slightly from the lecturer's scores, but the method still provides a framework for quantitative evaluation.
Evaluating the fine-tuned model on the entire test set gives an average score just above 50, or about 55%, which is not very good because some answers are correct and some are wrong.
A model error can occur when the response simply repeats the input instead of performing the requested rewrite.
The model's performance can be improved by adjusting hyperparameters such as the learning rate, batch size, or number of epochs.
The training dataset used here was small, with 1100 instruction-input-output pairs in total and only about 800 pairs used for training because 85% of the data was used as training data.
The model's performance can be improved by increasing the size of the training dataset.
The Stanford Alpaca repository contains a dataset of 52,000 instruction-output pairs, which is about 50 times larger than the dataset used here, and using such a dataset may produce better responses.
The model's responses can be guided more effectively by experimenting with different prompts or instruction formats.
Using a larger pre-trained model may improve accuracy because it has greater capacity to capture complex patterns and generate more accurate responses.

In this lecture the model used was GPT-2 Medium with 355 million parameters, and larger alternatives mentioned were GPT-2 Large with 774 million parameters and GPT-2 XL with more than a billion parameters.
Larger models should be used only if sufficient compute power or GPU access is available.
For example, GPT-2 XL has 48 transformer layers and 25 attention heads in each transformer.
The fine-tuning technique shown here is standard full fine-tuning, where all parameters in the architecture are updated based on the specific dataset.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning refers to methods such as LoRA that make fine-tuning more efficient than normal full fine-tuning.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning can provide substantial computational speedup and can sometimes also improve accuracy.
Three evaluation methods for instruction-fine-tuned LLMs are MMLU, human preference comparison, and using another larger language model to evaluate the model's performance.
MMLU measures Massive Multitask Language Understanding.
Human preference comparison means asking humans to rate LLM output.
In this lecture, the model was evaluated by using another larger language model, specifically the Meta Llama 8B Instruct model, as an automated and simpler evaluation method.
Benchmarks such as MMLU are worth using because they are impactful and highly relevant for learning and for contributing to LLM evaluation research.

The lecture's instruction fine-tuning pipeline included preparing the dataset, fine-tuning the large language model, extracting responses, doing qualitative evaluation, and doing quantitative scoring using Ollama.
Through this process, the lecture also introduced a new tool called Ollama.
